sec: Atheroembolic renal disease: mechanism & clinical features · p803

items.q: Athero-embolic renal disease is also known as:
items.exp: Athero-embolic renal disease AKA cholesterol embolism, seen in patients with extensive aortic atherosclerosis. (Book p803)

items.q: Which patient is most at risk of athero-embolic renal disease?
opts: Extensive aortic atherosclerosis after endovascular intervention
A young patient with nephrotic syndrome and a normal aorta
A patient with recurrent urinary tract infections and pyuria
A patient with ADPKD and recurrent cyst haemorrhage
items.exp: Athero-embolic renal disease occurs in patients with extensive aortic atherosclerosis after endovascular intervention — angiography, anticoagulation, thrombolysis, surgery — or spontaneously. (Book p803)

items.q: Match the triggers of athero-embolism — 1) Angiography  2) Anticoagulation  3) Thrombolysis  4) Surgery … A) All are listed triggers  B) None is a listed trigger
opts: All four are listed triggers, along with spontaneous occurrence
items.exp: Triggers (after endovascular intervention): angiography, anticoagulation, thrombolysis, surgery — or spontaneous. (Book p803)

items.q: Complete the pathophysiology of athero-embolic renal disease — 1) Atherosclerotic plaque  2) Consequence  3) Vessel calibre affected … A) Multiple small vessel occlusion (no large vessel occlusion)  B) Breaks off  C) Embolize distally
items.exp: Pathophysiology: atherosclerotic plaque breaks off → embolizes distally → multiple small vessel occlusion (no large vessel occlusion). (Book p803)

items.q: Athero-embolic renal disease causes multiple small vessel occlusions rather than occlusion of a large vessel.
opts: False — it occludes the main renal artery
False — it causes renal vein thrombosis
items.exp: Pathophysiology: plaque breaks off, embolizes distally and causes multiple small vessel occlusion — with no large vessel occlusion. (Book p803)

items.q: A patient develops renal failure over several weeks after cardiac catheterisation. Which feature of athero-embolic renal disease fits?
opts: Subacute renal failure over several weeks, with renal involvement in 75%
Abrupt anuric renal failure within 2 hours
items.exp: Clinical features: subacute renal failure over several weeks — 75% renal involvement. (Book p803)

items.q: In the clinical-features list, renal involvement in athero-embolic renal disease occurs in:
items.exp: Clinical features: subacute renal failure over several weeks with 75% renal involvement. (Book p803)

items.q: Match each clinical sign of athero-embolism with its site — 1) Skin  2) Retina  3) Gut … A) Hollenhorst plaque  B) Blue toe syndrome and livedo reticularis  C) Mesenteric ischemia
items.exp: Clinical features: skin — blue toe syndrome and livedo reticularis; retina — Hollenhorst plaque; and mesenteric ischemia. (Book p803)

items.q: Fill up: The retinal finding in athero-embolic renal disease is a ______ plaque.
items.exp: Retinal finding: Hollenhorst plaque, shown in the fundus figure of athero-embolic renal disease. (Book p803)

items.q: A 68-year-old man with aortic atherosclerosis has blue toes, livedo reticularis and a Hollenhorst plaque. What is the renal prognosis?
opts: Increased risk of ESRD with an overall poor prognosis
Progression to ESRD is prevented by statins
Only the skin is involved; kidneys are spared
items.exp: Clinical features of athero-embolic renal disease end with ↑risk of ESRD (end stage renal disease) and poor prognosis. (Book p803)

items.q: All but one of the following are clinical features of athero-embolic renal disease. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Blue toe syndrome with livedo reticularis
Subacute renal failure developing over several weeks
items.exp: Features listed: subacute renal failure over weeks (75% renal), blue toe syndrome, livedo reticularis, mesenteric ischemia, Hollenhorst plaque, ↑ESRD risk and poor prognosis. (Book p803)
